tier_reason: In the buger/jsonparser README Benchmarks tables, tidwall/gjson and 'encoding/json struct' both run in the same harness. The code is public: benchmark/benchmark_gjson_sonic_test.go (BenchmarkGjsonSmall/Medium/Large) and BenchmarkEncodingJsonStruct* in benchmark/benchmark_{small,medium,large}_payload_test.go. The page states the command (`go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5`, median of 5), Go 1.26.3 (matching benchmark/go.mod) and the CPU (Apple M4 Max), so code, compiler, flags and CPU are all present.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Small payload (190B): 402 ns/op vs encoding/json struct 1,300 ns/op (~3.2x faster); medium (2.4KB): 2,241 vs 9,911 ns/op (~4.4x); large (24KB): 22,756 vs 130,565 ns/op (~5.7x faster). ns/op values are verbatim from the page tables; the ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from a competitor's suite, the buger/jsonparser README, which gjson's author did not tune. The methodology is fully documented (Go 1.26.3, Apple M4 Max ARM64, median of 5), and benchmark/go.mod resolves gjson v1.19.0. The benchmarks are not like-for-like: the encoding/json baseline fully unmarshals into a typed struct, while gjson does lazy path lookups (one GetBytes per field) and reads only the requested fields. gjson allocates more than jsonparser (28,672 B/op on the large payload vs 4,432 for encoding/json). The hardware is Apple-silicon ARM64 only. gjson's own README gives a first-party corroboration: GJSONGet 202.1 ns/op vs JSONUnmarshalStruct 3219 ns/op, on an M1 Max with Go 1.22, code at tidwall/gjson-benchmarks.

notes: Every number matches gjson's own rows on the jsonparser page, and the metadata checks out: MIT, 15,559 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-08-28, active. I fixed the speedup label to mark the ratios as derived and set compared_against_cpp_std_directly to false, because the baseline is Go's encoding/json and not a C++ standard library.

tier_reason: kostya/benchmarks is an independent third-party suite (2.9k stars). Its Json table has Scala (jsoniter-scala) at 0.147±0.001 s, C++/g++ (RapidJSON) at 0.154±0.001 s and C++/clang++ (RapidJSON) at 0.194±0.001 s. The code is public (json/json-scala/src/main/scala/JsonTest.scala, json/test_rapid.cpp, json/Makefile), the flags are in common/commands.mk, and the README's Environment section gives the compiler versions (Scala 3.8.4, gcc 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8) and the CPU (Xeon E-2324G). Everything tier A needs is present.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Scala 3.8.4: plain `scalac` (no extra options) compiles json/json-scala/src/main/scala/JsonTest.scala against jsoniter-scala-macros_3 2.39.1 (json/json-scala/Maven.list, fetched with coursier). The classes go into a fat jar built by common/jvm/combinejars.sh (not sbt-assembly), which runs as `scala application.jar` under xtime.rb. RapidJSON (a clone of miloyip/rapidjson) builds with g++ 16.1.0 as `g++ $(COMMON_FLAGS) -std=c++23` and with clang++ 22.1.8 as `clang++ $(COMMON_FLAGS) -std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++`. COMMON_FLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk). README results are dated UPDATE: 2026-07-19.
corrections.workload: Parse /tmp/1.json and average the x/y/z coordinates. json/generate_json.rb generates the file as a pretty-printed object: 'coordinates' holds 524,288 records, each with x/y/z doubles, a 'name' string and a nested 'opts' object. The timed window, bracketed by notify start/stop, excludes process/JVM startup, file loading and a two-tiny-document self-test. It runs on the same machine and Docker image as the C++ entries.
corrections.caveats: The win over RapidJSON(g++) is small: 0.147 vs 0.154 s, ~1.05x. The comparison is not like-for-like in two ways. jsoniter-scala uses a compile-time typed case-class codec that decodes only x/y/z and skips name/opts, while RapidJSON builds a full DOM. The RapidJSON rows also use its default, less precise number parsing. Against RapidJSON Precise (0.212 s g++, 0.262 s clang++), jsoniter-scala leads by ~1.44x/1.78x (derived from page data). The Scala row uses more energy than g++ RapidJSON (7.89 J vs 6.61 J) and more memory (283.94+25.62 MiB vs 113.21+123.44 MiB). JIT warm-up is only the two tiny self-test calls, so this is a single-shot run, not steady-state throughput. Several C/C++ parsers are faster on the same page: simdjson On-Demand at 0.060 s, DAW JSON Link, gason and yyjson. The suite pins jsoniter-scala 2.39.1, while the current release is v2.41.1 (2026-09-25). The workload is a single synthetic one.

notes: The three times match the page exactly and the derived ~1.05x-1.32x is correct. Metadata is correct: MIT, 819 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-09-25, active. I corrected the build description, because the suite uses scalac, coursier and combinejars.sh, not sbt-assembly, and gave the full COMMON_FLAGS. I set compared_against_cpp_std_directly to false, because RapidJSON is a third-party C++ library and not a C++ standard library.

tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section compares jsonparser with 'encoding/json struct' on the 190B, 2.4KB and 24KB payloads. The code is public: BenchmarkJsonParser* and BenchmarkEncodingJsonStruct* in benchmark/benchmark_{small,medium,large}_payload_test.go. The command (`go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5`, median of 5), Go 1.26.3 (benchmark/go.mod: go 1.26.3) and the CPU (Apple M4 Max) are stated. The numbers are first-party, but full methodology meets tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Large payload (24KB): 20,114 ns/op vs encoding/json struct 130,565 ns/op, '6.5x faster than encoding/json' (verbatim from page), with 0 B/op and 0 allocs/op vs 4,432 B/op and 147 allocs/op. Small payload (190B), EachKey: 227 vs 1,300 ns/op (~5.7x faster, derived from page data). Medium (2.4KB): EachKey 1,657 and Get 3,141 vs 9,911 ns/op (~6.0x and ~3.2x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is first-party (the project's own repo), but the methodology (hardware, Go version, run count) is fully stated, so it is treated as Tier A. The numbers are Apple-silicon ARM64, not the x86 hardware most servers run. The comparison is not like-for-like: encoding/json fully unmarshals into a typed struct, while jsonparser scans bytes and extracts only the requested fields. The result depends on the API used: on the medium payload, Get (3,141 ns/op) is slower than gjson (2,241), easyjson (2,368) and sonic (2,703), and only EachKey (1,657) leads. On the small payload, EachObject (205 ns/op) allocates 64 B/op.

notes: Every figure appears in the README tables. The 6.5x large-payload figure is the page's own claim, and I relabelled the small-payload ~5.7x as derived. Metadata is correct: MIT, 5,657 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-08-21, active. I set compared_against_cpp_std_directly to false, because the baseline is Go's encoding/json.
